transcripts.transcript: Imagine you apply for a new job, get invited for an interview, and your first conversation with the company is with a computer. Before a real person listens to you, an AI system analyses the stream of your data and generates a report. Only then will the recruiters decide whether you get a rejection letter or go to the next round. That is because companies are using AI to reduce costs and make HR processes more efficient. Although this can be good for business, it feels dystopian to be analysed by a machine. The main problem with automated decision making systems or ADM is that their algorithms and criteria are not always transparent, and they can analyse things like your facial expressions, gestures or tone of voice to make their decisions. Sometimes not even the creators know what the criteria are, since AI is a self-learning system that is constantly updated. The result can be making the current disparities of our society even worse. Bad patterns can be replicated by the machines if the training data and people who make decisions related to AI do not focus on equality and diversity. For instance, if a job has traditionally been dominated by one gender, AI will keep repeating that. Some AI systems use predictive technologies that can pose privacy issues. For example, AI can analyse a candidate's tone of voice or appearance to predict factors like depression or medical conditions, which should not be considered in hiring. Just like European users have their data protected by the GDPR law, applicants must be able to decide whether or not they want to be evaluated by AI. Also, the criteria used by AI must be transparent and allow appealing in case of mistakes, so the system can be trusted and the candidates have the chance to improve. But AI can also help who's looking for a job. Tools like Chat GPT can help organise your work experience in cover letters and CVs by using important keywords and correcting typing mistakes. You can also simulate an interview and get feedback on your skills. But although it can help, it doesn't do miracles, but you are the one who knows how to best present yourself. Our working life is each day more affected by AI and soon most jobs will have some influence from these systems. The main tension is between having AI focused on raising profits or using AI to empower workers. Solving this requires a collective effort, so we can have transparency, fair representation and shared responsibility. You can help in many ways, like getting involved in the Works council, the trainee representation, or a trade union. Additionally, you can advocate against algorithm-based discrimination through socio-political engagement. Go visit democracyAI.EU and learn more about it with more videos and a free online course.
